Second definition of `self.downsize` overwrites the 4-argument overload

Defining `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149 overwrites `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` on line 145. `include_website_name` is missing `?` and bypasses `untrusted_attributes` restrictions

`ActiveModel::Serializer` expects conditional inclusion methods to end with a question mark (`include_website_name?`). As a result, a TL0 user's website host/path is still exposed in the JSON and rendered as text on the user profile page for anonymous users. true_positives.matched_candidate:
`FallbackLocaleList#[]` does not normalize `locale` to a symbol

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` without converting `locale` to a symbol. When `locale` is passed as a `String` (for example via `I18n.t(key, locale: "en")` or `I18n.fallbacks["en"]`), `.uniq` will not deduplicate `"en"` against `:en` (returning `["en", :en]`), and `I18n.load_locale` will not match `"en"` against `:en` in `@loaded_locales`, causing all YAML files for that locale to be parsed and loaded a second time.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback and explicit `:locale` translations are not loaded outside `ApplicationController#set_locale` or after `I18n.reload!`

`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is only invoked in `ApplicationController#set_locale`, while `I18n.translate` in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb` still only runs `load_locale(config.locale)`. Because `translate_accelerator.rb` overrides `I18n::Backend::Base#load_translations` to prevent automatic loading, `I18n.backend` only contains translations for locales explicitly passed to `load_locale`. Consequently:
1. Any translation call outside a controller request (such as in Sidekiq background jobs, `UserNotifications` mailers, rake tasks, or specs) or after `I18n.reload!` is called will only load `config.locale` and leave the fallback locales (`SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`) unloaded. Fallback lookups will fail with `"translation missing"` and cache the missing-translation string in `@cache`.
2. Calling `I18n.t(key, locale: other_locale)` when `other_locale` has not yet been loaded will not load `other_locale` at all; with `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` enabled, it will silently return the `:en` / `SiteSetting.default_locale` fallback even when a translation exists for `other_locale`.

Missing specs for server-side locale fallbacks

This PR introduces custom server-side locale fallback ordering (`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`) and lazy fallback loading via `FallbackLocaleList`, but adds no specs verifying fallback lookup behavior, pluralization fallback behavior, or lazy loading of fallback locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Consumer group rebalance shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool and causes all subsequent messages to be dropped and committed

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance for the lifetime of the factory, and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` passes that shared `self.queue_pool` into each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions()`. In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka partition rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` closes or terminates the active `ProcessingStrategy` (`strategy.close()` / `strategy.join()` / `strategy.terminate()`) and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions()` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` both call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, the first rebalance permanently shuts down all queues (`q.shutdown()`) and exits all worker threads on `self.queue_pool`. On the new strategy created after the rebalance, every `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()` on a shut-down queue, raising `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception`, logs it, and calls `add_offset()` + `complete_offset()`, so the consumer will silently drop 100% of messages after any rebalance while committing their offsets to Kafka. In addition, `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker` retains state from revoked partitions across rebalances, causing the commit thread to commit offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops the commit thread before workers finish

There are two ordering defects in shutdown handling:
1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all `OrderedQueueWorker` instances before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits immediately after finishing its current item instead of draining the remaining items in `self.work_queue` until `queue.ShutDown` is raised. Any queued items are abandoned with their offsets still in `offset_tracker.outstanding`.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `self.shutdown_event` and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, with no final commit afterward. Offsets completed by workers while `queue_pool.shutdown()` is draining/joining are never committed to Kafka. (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` also does not join `self.commit_thread`, and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` shuts down `queue_pool` without stopping `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.commit_thread`.)

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets skips over offset gaps after mark_committed prunes all_offsets

In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`, the contiguous scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. However, `mark_committed(partition, offset)` removes all offsets `<= offset` from `self.all_offsets[partition]`. As a result, once an offset has been committed, every remaining entry in `all_offsets` is strictly greater than `last_committed`, making `min_offset >= last_committed + 1` always true for monotonically increasing offsets. If there is a gap (e.g. offsets 100, 102, 103 are completed while 101 is still missing), the first call to `get_committable_offsets()` returns 100 and `mark_committed(partition, 100)` leaves `all_offsets = {102, 103}` and `last_committed = 100`. On the very next commit loop iteration, `min_offset` is 102, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`, causing the tracker to jump over the missing offset 101 and commit 103. When `partition in self.last_committed`, `start` must be `self.last_committed[partition] + 1`, only using `min_offset` when no offset has been committed for that partition yet.

Worker queues are unbounded and provide no backpressure to Arroyo StreamProcessor

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` in a tight loop until `MessageRejected` is raised. Because `work_queue.put()` never blocks or rejects, if worker processing falls behind Kafka consumption, the consumer will buffer an unbounded number of `WorkItem` and `Message` objects in memory. Furthermore, if a bounded queue were used, the broad `except Exception:` handler in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` (lines 317-325) would catch `queue.Full` / `MessageRejected` and immediately mark the unqueued message's offset as completed instead of propagating `MessageRejected` to Arroyo.

On the new strategy created after the rebalance, every `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()` on a shut-down queue, raising `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception`, logs it, and calls `add_offset()` + `complete_offset()`, so the consumer will silently drop 100% of messages after any rebalance while committing their offsets to Kafka. As a result, once an offset has been committed, every remaining entry in `all_offsets` is strictly greater than `last_committed`, making `min_offset >= last_committed + 1` always true for monotonically increasing offsets. If there is a gap (e.g. offsets 100, 102, 103 are completed while 101 is still missing), the first call to `get_committable_offsets()` returns 100 and `mark_committed(partition, 100)` leaves `all_offsets = {102, 103}` and `last_committed = 100`. On the very next commit loop iteration, `min_offset` is 102, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`, causing the tracker to jump over the missing offset 101 and commit 103. When `partition in self.last_committed`, `start` must be `self.last_committed[partition] + 1`, only using `min_offset` when no offset has been committed for that partition yet.

Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits immediately after finishing its current item instead of draining the remaining items in `self.work_queue` until `queue.ShutDown` is raised. Any queued items are abandoned with their offsets still in `offset_tracker.outstanding`.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `self.shutdown_event` and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, with no final commit afterward. Offsets completed by workers while `queue_pool.shutdown()` is draining/joining are never committed to Kafka. Because `work_queue.put()` never blocks or rejects, if worker processing falls behind Kafka consumption, the consumer will buffer an unbounded number of `WorkItem` and `Message` objects in memory. Furthermore, if a bounded queue were used, the broad `except Exception:` handler in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` (lines 317-325) would catch `queue.Full` / `MessageRejected` and immediately mark the unqueued message's offset as completed instead of propagating `MessageRejected` to Arroyo.

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` instance for the lifetime of the factory, and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` passes that shared `self.queue_pool` into each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions()`. In Arroyo, whenever a Kafka partition rebalance occurs, `StreamProcessor` closes or terminates the active `ProcessingStrategy` (`strategy.close()` / `strategy.join()` / `strategy.terminate()`) and then calls `factory.create_with_partitions()` for the new assignment. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` both call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, the first rebalance permanently shuts down all queues (`q.shutdown()`) and exits all worker threads on `self.queue_pool`. On the new strategy created after the rebalance, every `submit()` call hits `work_queue.put()` on a shut-down queue, raising `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches `Exception`, logs it, and calls `add_offset()` + `complete_offset()`, so the consumer will silently drop 100% of messages after any rebalance while committing their offsets to Kafka. In addition, `self.queue_pool.offset_tracker` retains state from revoked partitions across rebalances, causing the commit thread to commit offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own.

In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`, the contiguous scan starts at `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. However, `mark_committed(partition, offset)` removes all offsets `<= offset` from `self.all_offsets[partition]`. As a result, once an offset has been committed, every remaining entry in `all_offsets` is strictly greater than `last_committed`, making `min_offset >= last_committed + 1` always true for monotonically increasing offsets. If there is a gap (e.g. offsets 100, 102, 103 are completed while 101 is still missing), the first call to `get_committable_offsets()` returns 100 and `mark_committed(partition, 100)` leaves `all_offsets = {102, 103}` and `last_committed = 100`. On the very next commit loop iteration, `min_offset` is 102, so `start = max(101, 102) = 102`, causing the tracker to jump over the missing offset 101 and commit 103. When `partition in self.last_committed`, `start` must be `self.last_committed[partition] + 1`, only using `min_offset` when no offset has been committed for that partition yet.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued items and stops the commit thread before workers finish

1. `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all `OrderedQueueWorker` instances before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits immediately after finishing its current item instead of draining the remaining items in `self.work_queue` until `queue.ShutDown` is raised. Any queued items are abandoned with their offsets still in `offset_tracker.outstanding`.
2. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` sets `self.shutdown_event` and joins `self.commit_thread` *before* calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, with no final commit afterward. Offsets completed by workers while `queue_pool.shutdown()` is draining/joining are never committed to Kafka. (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` also does not join `self.commit_thread`, and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` shuts down `queue_pool` without stopping `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.commit_thread`.)

Worker queues are unbounded and provide no backpressure to Arroyo StreamProcessor

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring states that it provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each `queue.Queue()` with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka and calls `strategy.submit(message)` in a tight loop until `MessageRejected` is raised. Because `work_queue.put()` never blocks or rejects, if worker processing falls behind Kafka consumption, the consumer will buffer an unbounded number of `WorkItem` and `Message` objects in memory. Furthermore, if a bounded queue were used, the broad `except Exception:` handler in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` (lines 317-325) would catch `queue.Full` / `MessageRejected` and immediately mark the unqueued message's offset as completed instead of propagating `MessageRejected` to Arroyo.
